title: DIRECTIVE, METACOGNITIVE OR A BLEND OF BOTH? A COMPARISON OF AI-GENERATED FEEDBACK TYPES ON STUDENT ENGAGEMENT, CONFIDENCE, AND OUTCOMES
extended_summary:
This paper examines how different types of AI-generated feedback affect student engagement, confidence, and learning outcomes in higher education. The authors focus on a longstanding instructional design question: whether students benefit more from directive feedback that tells them what to change, metacognitive feedback that prompts reflection and self-regulated learning, or a hybrid approach that combines both. The study aims to move beyond theory and small-scale prior work by directly comparing these feedback types in an authentic course setting.

The intervention was implemented in RiPPLE, an adaptive educational platform used in a university design and programming course. Students created learning resources such as multiple-choice questions and received one of three AI-generated feedback conditions: directive, metacognitive, or hybrid. The feedback was standardized so that only the suggestions-for-improvement section differed by condition. The study analyzed linguistic differences in the feedback itself, student engagement time, whether students revised their work after feedback, confidence ratings, and final resource quality.

The population consisted of 329 students in a semester-long introductory university course at The University of Queensland. Most participants were undergraduates, with a smaller number of postgraduate and non-award students. The intervention ran over a 12-week semester and was embedded in normal coursework through three four-week collaborative learning rounds. Students used the platform online as part of their course requirements.

The main findings were that the three AI feedback types were linguistically distinct as designed, and that feedback type significantly influenced revision behavior. Hybrid feedback led to the most revision activity, metacognitive feedback led to the least, and directive feedback fell in between but was also significantly more likely than metacognitive feedback to prompt revisions. However, there were no significant differences across conditions in engagement time, confidence, or final resource quality. The authors conclude that hybrid AI feedback is especially promising because it combines actionable guidance with reflective prompting, supporting revision behavior without reducing confidence or outcomes.

identified_tools.name: RiPPLE
identified_tools.description: RiPPLE is an adaptive educational platform for student co-creation of learning resources, peer evaluation, adaptive practice, and AI-supported oversight.
identified_tools.use_case: RiPPLE served as the experimental platform in a semester-long randomized controlled trial where students received AI-generated directive, metacognitive, or hybrid feedback on educational resources they created.

findings.finding_summary: In the RCT with 329 students, action on feedback differed significantly by condition, with students in the Metacognitive condition revising least often (12.1%) versus Directive (21.1%) and Hybrid (27.5%). A logistic mixed-effects model showed an overall condition effect, χ2(2)=8.74, p=.013; Directive vs. Metacognitive OR=2.93, 95% CI [1.25, 6.88], p=.009, and Hybrid had about 4.3 times higher odds of revision than Metacognitive, 95% CI [1.82, 10.0], p<.001, while Directive vs. Hybrid was not significant (OR=0.69, 95% CI [0.32, 1.48], p=.484).
findings.measure: Revision/action on feedback after receiving AI-generated feedback
findings.effect_size: OR=2.93 (Directive vs. Metacognitive); OR=0.69 (Directive vs. Hybrid); Hybrid about 4.3 times higher odds than Metacognitive
findings.confidence_interval: Directive vs. Metacognitive 95% CI [1.25, 6.88]; Directive vs. Hybrid 95% CI [0.32, 1.48]; Metacognitive vs. Hybrid 95% CI [0.10, 0.55]

findings.finding_summary: Engagement time did not differ significantly across feedback conditions in the RCT. Estimated marginal means were 107.9 seconds for Directive (95% CI [94.0, 124.0]), 87.4 seconds for Metacognitive (95% CI [76.1, 100.0]), and 97.8 seconds for Hybrid (95% CI [85.3, 112.0]); the overall Gamma GLMM effect was χ2(2)=4.48, p=.107.
findings.measure: Engagement time between feedback receipt and subsequent submission
findings.confidence_interval: Directive 95% CI [94.0, 124.0]; Metacognitive 95% CI [76.1, 100.0]; Hybrid 95% CI [85.3, 112.0]

findings.finding_summary: Confidence ratings were broadly similar across the three feedback conditions, with no statistically significant group differences. The CLMM showed χ2=.96, p=.62; back-transformed estimated means were 3.63 for Directive (95% CI [2.94, 4.32]), 3.25 for Metacognitive (95% CI [2.48, 4.02]), and 3.55 for Hybrid (95% CI [2.88, 4.23]).
findings.measure: Self-rated confidence/resource quality confidence on a 1-5 scale
findings.confidence_interval: Directive 95% CI [2.94, 4.32]; Metacognitive 95% CI [2.48, 4.02]; Hybrid 95% CI [2.88, 4.23]

findings.finding_summary: Resource outcome quality did not differ significantly by feedback condition. The beta GLMM showed χ2=1.40, p=.49; back-transformed estimated means were 3.62 for Directive (95% CI [3.45, 3.78]), 3.72 for Metacognitive (95% CI [3.55, 3.87]), and 3.75 for Hybrid (95% CI [3.59, 3.91]).
findings.confidence_interval: Directive 95% CI [3.45, 3.78]; Metacognitive 95% CI [3.55, 3.87]; Hybrid 95% CI [3.59, 3.91]

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI used to produce automated educational feedback, with no specific model or product identified in the paper.
identified_tools.use_case: The study compared three AI-generated feedback designs—directive, metacognitive, and hybrid—delivered to students on their created course resources within RiPPLE.

findings.finding_summary: The AI-generated feedback types were linguistically distinct in intended function. Reflective prompts per 100 words were highest in Metacognitive (M=4.45, SD=1.07), intermediate in Hybrid (M=2.20, SD=0.65), and near zero in Directive (M=0.01, SD=0.12), F(2,1024)=3329.39, p<.001, η2=.867; imperatives per 100 words were highest in Directive (M=2.91, SD=0.81), moderate in Hybrid (M=1.34, SD=0.52), and zero in Metacognitive, F(2,1024)=2340.75, p<.001, η2=.821.
findings.measure: Linguistic/structural features of AI-generated feedback text

findings.finding_summary: Feedback length also differed significantly by AI-generated feedback type. Hybrid feedback was longest (M=134.14 words, SD=17.66, 95% CI [132.23, 136.05]), Metacognitive was intermediate (M=97.10, SD=11.71), and Directive shortest (M=83.25, SD=15.63), with F(2,1024)=1019.56, p<.001, η2=.666; all Tukey pairwise contrasts were significant at adjusted p<.001.
findings.measure: Word count of AI-generated feedback text

quality_tier_rationale: This is a semester-long randomized controlled trial with 329 students in an authentic course setting, which is strong primary evidence. It is not blue because results are from a single higher-education context and several main learning outcomes were null, with some reporting limitations around effect sizes for those outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: The clearest impact was on revision behavior/action on feedback, where Hybrid and Directive outperformed Metacognitive, but confidence and resource quality showed no significant differences. Overall impact is therefore meaningful but limited and unclear for academic outcomes.
